value.overview: The Golden-bellied Flycatcher (Myiodynastes hemichrysus) is a large, boldly patterned tyrant flycatcher of humid mountain forests in Central America and northern South America. It is often recognized by its bright yellow underparts, dark head, pale eyebrow, and strong, slightly hooked bill. The species is usually encountered high in the canopy or along forest edges, where it watches from exposed perches and makes short flights to capture prey. Costa Rica is an important part of its northern range.
value.classification: The Golden-bellied Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Myiodynastes. It is closely related to other large, boldly marked flycatchers traditionally grouped as sulphur-bellied or streaked flycatchers.
value.identification: This is a fairly large flycatcher with a dark gray-brown head, a noticeable pale eyebrow, a heavy dark bill, and olive-brown upperparts. The throat is pale, while the breast and belly are rich yellow, usually with darker streaking across the upper breast and sides. The wings show contrasting rufous or cinnamon tones and pale edging. Its combination of yellow underparts, bold facial pattern, large bill, and montane forest habitat helps separate it from similar Myiodynastes flycatchers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama south through Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and northern Peru. In Costa Rica it is a resident of both slopes, from the Cordillera de Guanacaste southward, and is generally more frequent on the Caribbean slope. It inhabits montane evergreen forest, cloud forest, forest edges, and mature secondary forest, usually at roughly 700–1,850 meters. It may also occur in wooded gardens and disturbed areas retaining tall trees.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range; it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur with elevation or food availability, but seasonal migration is not well established.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of more widespread lowland flycatchers. The species forms territorial pairs during the breeding period and is believed to nest in natural cavities or other protected openings in trees, although detailed nest records are scarce. In Costa Rica, breeding activity is associated with the wetter part of the year in montane habitats, when insect and fruit resources are available. More field observations are needed to define nesting dates, nest structure, clutch size, and parental care.
value.dietFeeding: The Golden-bellied Flycatcher feeds mainly on large insects and other arthropods captured from exposed perches. It sallies into the canopy or forest edge to seize flying prey and may also glean food from foliage. Small fruits and berries are likely taken opportunistically, as in several related Myiodynastes flycatchers. Its large bill allows it to handle relatively substantial prey, and it often returns to the same perch after a short hunting flight.
value.behavior: It is usually seen alone or in pairs, perched quietly in the middle or upper canopy and scanning for prey. Short, direct sallies are commonly followed by a return to the same or a nearby perch. The species can be conspicuous when calling, but it may remain difficult to see in dense cloud forest. It defends feeding or breeding territories and may join mixed-species foraging groups occasionally, especially outside the breeding period.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population trend is not well documented, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
